notes.title: Nightly Penitence
notes.content:
Today, we’ll show you the WIP of this [b]quest marker[/b], for which we used this figure drawn in the Codex Borbonicus.

This figure represents the [b]night[/b] as an eye star surrounded by darkness, above two bloody [b]thorns [/b]which represented self-sacrifice and penitence. 

This icon could be interpreted as the blood poured over the heart of the night; namely, the "[i][b]nightly penitence[/b][/i]".

notes.title: The Ceiba tree
notes.content:
Greetings, dear [b]Mictecs[/b]!

Today we want to show you this [b]3D rendering[/b] of a monument built by the Secretary of Arts and Culture of Merida, Yucatan, honoring [b]Ceiba[/b], the world tree.

For pre-Columbian societies, the ceiba tree held the [b]universe in place[/b], which was why the gods planted 4 of them on each [b]cardinal point[/b], each of a different color: the black ceiba was west, the white ceiba on the north, the yellow ceiba south and the red on the east.

This way, the trees represented a [b]bridge [/b]between earth, heaven and the underworld, each made up by several levels: 13 for heaven and 9 for the underworld.

So tell us, what do you think of this homage to Merida, Yucatan?

notes.title: Calendar reading: a concept art
notes.content:
What is the [b]meaning of life[/b]? 

The unavoidable question that dives into the [b]uncertainty [/b]of the future; but pre-Columbian civilization had the certainty that the [b]will of the gods[/b] could manifest itself to us through [b]nature[/b]. 

Their worldview marked the time they lived in, and guided the action of every [b]Mexica[/b], forming what we now know as one of the greatest and most impressive cultures of the world.

Today we want to show you some of the [b]art [/b]created by members of the team behind [i]Mictlan[/i], where a child is brought to a sage to have their [b]calendar reading [/b]done. This 260-day calendar kept sacred dates, established harvest cycles, rains and droughts, read dreams, predicted wars and [b]prophesied the future[/b] of each Mecixa.

Are you ready to know what the gods have in store for you?

notes.title: "Cueitl" and "Hornettes"
notes.content:
Today we will show you this concept art on different [b]dresses [/b]and [b]hairstyles [/b]inspired by historical evidence as well as contemporary communities.

The base of the common everyday clothes of pre-Columbian people was a [b]cueitl[/b], a long rectangular cloak held at the waist with a [b]nelpiloni [/b](either a rope or a belt). 
Cueitl could be plain or decorated with lavish shapes depicting flowers and/or elaborate geometric designs.

These hairstyles were also specifically for women. The one we know the most of is one that historians have dubbed as “[b]hornettes[/b]”, which consisted of braiding the hair over the side of the forehead along with colored cotton thread, forming one braid on each side of the head, each ending with a small point on the top.

notes.title: Photogrammetry
notes.content:
Greetings, warriors!

In this special post, we will show you our team getting to work, led by our creative director [b]Guillermo Alarcón[/b]. 

As you already know, one of the graphic techniques used for creating the look and feel of [i]Micltan [/i]is [b]photogrammetry[/b]; with this method, we can capture and measure terrains, structures or people with [b]incredible precision[/b].

Here you can see a photoshoot with members of an [b]indigenous community [/b]that will be used to create hyper-realistic characters. 

[i]Mictlan [/i]is not only inspired by the past, but also by our common heritage.

notes.title: Temple of Xiuhtecuhtli
notes.content:
[i]Niltze[/i] (Hello), [b]Mictec family[/b]!

Today, the omens of an invasion manifest, and with it this #WIP of the [b]Temple of Xiuhtecuhtli [/b](the Old God, Lord of fire and heat).
Fatal auguries in the ancient codices tell of the coming of the Spanish, and in this occasion, we present to you the scene of the third sign: “[i]It didn’t rain hard, only drizzled slightly, and it wasn’t the heat from the sun, and there was no thunder either[/i]” This is what the inhabitants reported when they narrated how the sanctuary with a straw roof, called Xacal, burned up in flames.

What do you think, Mictecs? Do you know the other [b]fatal auguries[/b]?

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/18849f68ffe6cd62faf6604b007e68f6f8e64577.jpg[/img]

The [b]artistic expression[/b] of pre-Columbian culture didn’t have a limit: dance, music, painting and sculpture are some of the examples of the [b]ingenuity [/b]of our ancestors.
This WIP is part of the structure of the Temple of Xiuhtecuhtli, that sanctuary dedicated to the [b]God of Fire[/b]. The team of artists of Mictlan followed the ancient ways and recreated this sculpture that decorates the stairs of the sanctuary.

Did you like it? In [i]Mictlan [/i]we are interested in your opinions.

notes.title: Flyers of Papantla
notes.content:
Greetings, travelers of [i]Mictlan[/i]. It is with much pleasure that we present you this concept art, where you can see various reinterpretations of the [b]Flyers of Papantla[/b].

The Ritual of the Flyers, practiced in pre-Columbian times as a fertility ritual, was particularly important for the Aztecs. In this ritual the flyers danced in the air around a [b]human sacrifice[/b], a victim whose blood, when reaching the ground, assured a [b]bountiful harvest[/b].

While the fliers in bigger cities would have more ostentatious clothes, in this reinterpretation we can see them with simpler and more humble clothes, as they’re represented in the Codex Porfirio Díaz.

Which design do you like the most? [b]Tell us in the comments[/b]!

notes.title: Tlacatecolotl
notes.content:
In the original Nahua, [b]Tlacatecolotl [/b]means “Owl Man”: they are dark sorcerers, with the owl as their [b]nagual [/b]([url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3110297119570303839]we talked about this here[/url]), a harbinger of death and ill luck. 

They made a living from their [b]malicious arts[/b], usually cheating their victims, since they would cast spells on them only to charge exorbitant prices to lift the curses. 
It’s not surprising then, that pre-Columbian authorities would [b]persecute [/b]Tlacatecolotl, or even avoid their infamous services whenever possible.

In this WIP we can see the masked face of one of these fearsome [b]necromancers[/b], with his mask reminding of a great horned owl.

notes.title: Heart extraction
notes.content:
Sacrificial rituals featuring human [b]heart extraction [/b]were a prevalent religious practice throughout ancient Mesoamerican societies, it was a way of establishing a [b]mystic connection[/b] between humans and the gods.
Stories from both the oral tradition and chronicles of the time remark the importance of this practice: the sacrificed victims were either [b]volunteers [/b]or [b]prisoners [/b]captured in the Flower Wars.

Here is a concept art piece from our talented team:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/7995e08b5a9a3839a071a1965932936071c4ea6c.jpg[/img]

Human sacrifices were usually performed at[b] sunrise [/b]or at [b]midday[/b], in accordance with the belief that blood replenished the solar cycle that gives life to the world.
However, there was a very special ceremony that was performed at [b]midnight[/b].

The ritual of [b]New Fire [/b]was celebrated every 52 years on the Huizachtepet, today called [i]Cerro de la Estrella[/i] (Hill of the Star), on Iztapalapa, in order to bless the coming Period; in this ritual, a human victim was offered, but only after all the [b]fires [/b]on all of Tenochtitlan and its surroundings were [b]put out[/b]. 

Once the sacrifice was completed, a fire was lit over the victim's head, which would then be shared throughout the city while everyone anxiously awaited the break of a new dawn, which would kickstart the next [b]52-years period[/b] and the endurance of the [b]Fifth Sun[/b].

notes.title: We keep expanding Mictlan
notes.content:
Reconstructing the ancient mythical tales of ancient México, it’s [b]not an easy task[/b].

Our [b]team of historians [/b]and archaeologists analyze the ancient monuments and historical evidence, then our [b]concept art team[/b] reconstructs Mesoamerican iconography and architecture mixing historical and fantasy elements to give life to ancient Mesoamerica in the 16th century! 

We’ve currently made[b] over 85 real-life-looking [/b] humans, monsters and mythical creature characters.
We've also created dozens of ancient [b]archaeological sites[/b] in Unreal Engine, sites from Tulum, Tenochtitlan, Tenochtitlan, Cholula and more, all within the expanded 45KM 2 square[b] open-world map [/b]of ancient Mexico (soon expanding to Central America!)

All of this in just less than 1 year in full development, including a 15-minute gameplay video ([url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3110297119570368253]have you seen it?[/url])!
Not bad for an indie studio with a low budget. Our strength is [b]our passion[/b] and [b]our community[/b]!

notes.title: The Chichimec
notes.content:
Today we’ll show you this WIP of a study of the [b]Chichimec facial paint[/b].
The Chichimec were a group of nomadic and semi-nomadic people that inhabited the territory known as Gran Chichimeca.
These feared Mesoamerican people were known for the human and animal [b]sacrifices [/b]that they practiced, as well as for their [b]skill [/b]and fierceness in war. 
They dressed with little clothing and body paint, and their warriors went to battle with face paintings (usually in white colors) to [b]intimidate their enemies[/b].

notes.title: Just a catch up
notes.content:
At [i]Mictlan[/i], every day we challenge ourselves as we try to improve our work pipeline.

When we started the project, our knowledge was very basic, but little by little we have improved the way we work as a team. [i]Mictlan [/i]is our first video game, most of our team does not have professional industry experience, making our efforts even more difficult. 
But the need to improve and learn our way of working has helped us to grow a lot, experimenting over and over again until we find favorable results. On one hand, this process delays our project, but on the other hand, ensures that we have the exact results that we are aiming for. 

[h3]We might be a small studio, but we have big aspirations![/h3]
 
The response of our community, your comments, your constructive feedback has also helped us a lot to improve our way of working and give ourselves new perspectives. We want to thank you for being here from the very beginning, for all the good vibes and constant support you've been providing us.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/165ca5dbae2e4eff8206200603e4e4004e9a9689.png[/img]

notes.title: Black Temple
notes.content:
Today we are presenting concept art pieces of the[b] Black Temple[/b], right out of the imagination of our talented artist [b]Mauricio Pampin[/b].

In this temple, [b]Micltantecutli[/b]’s priests would worship him by sacrificing prisoners.
We can see where the points of interest will be located in the temple, like the sacrificial table or Mictlantecuhtli’s effigy, as well as the scale of the walls and columns in relation to the player’s character.

In order to accomplish this kind of works, our artists need to carry extensive research on [b]pre-Columbian architecture[/b], and then mix reality and historical accuracy with the[b] dark fantasy elements[/b] that will give this place a surreal, frightening look.

When you, the player, will descend into the [b]deepest and darkest[/b] levels of Mictlan, you will have to face several challenges and enemies... Mictecs are among the [b]greatest threats[/b].

notes.title: Two great temples
notes.content:
Today we want to show you some sketches from the megalithic [b]temple of Malinalco[/b], how it could have looked in its prime.
Malinalco was an [b]ideological and spiritual center[/b] for the Mexica Empire; it was the place where the sister of Huitzilopochtli, Malinalochitl, had settled when abandoned by his brother during a long pilgrimage of the Aztec people to the Valley of Mexico. And in this specific place, they prepared and commanded the eagle and jaguar warriors, the [b]elite militia[/b] from the Mexica army.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/283acf3e5c8b1d1918cada71f14e9124f59851d1.jpg[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/2cd5c828462d39771e2f90a1a24b3ef0d92f63d7.jpg[/img]

We also want to share with you the excellent work from our friend and collaborator [b]Mauricio Pampin[/b], who, on the basis of the postclassic aesthetic, built from zero a [b]great temple dedicated to Mictlantecuhtli[/b].
We know that the sanctuaries of Tenochtitlan played an important role, not only in the sacred area. In the “Calpulli” slums, sacred houses were built for the gods, where they held rituals to maintain the balance of the world.

notes.title: Xipe Totec
notes.content:
[b]Travelers of the underworld[/b]!

This is a new [b]variant [/b]we're working on to create[b] Xipe Totec[/b]. 

Our artists are constantly working, as they add [b]details[/b] to their models on the basis of the indications of our [b]historians [/b]and archeology team. 
What we're aiming for is a balance between [b]history and fantasy[/b], creating memorable characters for you to enjoy, with unique characteristics and visual elements!

Xipe Totec was a [b]life-death-rebirth deity[/b], god of agriculture, of spring and new vegetation.  Xipe Totec wore the [b]skin of a human victim[/b] as the symbol of a “new skin”, the "new skin" that covered the Earth in the [b]spring[/b].

notes.title: Stone Gloves
notes.content:
We have been working on developing a character whose main weapons are [b]stone gloves[/b], but do you know what did the pre-Hispanic gloves look like?

To answer this question, we must go back to the amazing work of [b]Taube and Zender[/b], [i]American gladiators: ritualistic boxing in ancient Mesoamerica[/i], where we can find several representations of brawlers and gloves made out of [b]shells, bones or stone[/b].

The use of these gloves is shared among the Olmec, Zapotec and Maya cultures and it is also featured in the outfit of some [b]gods [/b]such as Chaac, who wears a great stone glove which he uses to[b] light up the sky [/b]during storms.

notes.title: Xipe Totec
notes.content:
The cult of [b]Xipe Totec [/b]is one of the [b]oldest [/b]as well as one of the most [b]multifaceted [/b]that ever existed in ancient Mexico. 

Its appearance not only alluded to the [b]renewal [/b]of the land but also to [b]warfare[/b]. Xipe Totec [b]flayed himself[/b] to give food to humanity.

Without his skin, he was depicted as a [b]golden god[/b].

We opted for this representation to highlight the[b] fearsome aspect [/b]of this deity. Of course, this is still a [b]WIP [/b]and the final result will likely go through changes during our development process.

notes.title: Tlazolteotl
notes.content:
[b]Tlazolteotl[/b] (originally a deity of Huasteco origin) found a relevant place among the Mexica deities. She represented the different forms of [b]passion[/b], and that is why she was the goddess of [b]fertility [/b]and births.

Her help was sought as a goddess of carnal love, but it could cause unbridled[b] sexual appetites[/b]. She protected midwives and pregnant women, and her image was placed at the entrance of the temazcales where she was called “[b]Grandmother of temazcal[/b]”.

She was related to the goddess [b]Toci[/b], the mother of the gods, also known as "Heart of the earth" or "Entrails of the earth" because she [b]fostered life[/b] and cared for her children (gods, men, animals or plants).

Tlazolteotl was also know as "[b]Eater of filth"[/b] since she had the ability to [b]purify[/b] the bodies of sexual offenders if they performed acts of confession and sacrifice. As a matter of fact, Tlazoteotl is often depicted with her mouth and chin darkened from [b]consuming filth and sins[/b].

notes.title: Mictlan's weapons
notes.content:
Today we want to show you a set of designs of the[b] indigenous weapons [/b]that have been recreated by our concept artists.

Did you know about the lethality of the indigenous weapons in the pre-Hispanic world? 
[b]Let us tell you about it[/b]!

The many weapons that the indigenous people wielded needed to be mastered in order to be used to their [b]full potential[/b]; which is why the younger people were trained in their use from a relatively[b] early age[/b].

The [b]atlatl[/b], the[b] stone axes[/b], the [b]macuahuitl [/b]and the [b]obsidian knives[/b], are some of the weapons recorded by the chroniclers and researchers, who highlighted the remarkable characteristics of obsidian, deadly because of its sharpness and its splinters.

In [i]Mictlan [/i]you will be able to find these weapons and master them, to open your way through the deep underworld while you face [b]Spaniards[/b], rival [b]indigenous people[/b] and [b]supernatural creatures [/b]of Mesoamerican mythology.

notes.title: Incense for the deities
notes.content:
Did you know that the Mexica priests had to light up [b]incense [/b]for the effigies of their gods[b] four times a day[/b]?

Among the many tasks they had, the Mexica novices and priests were in charge of burning a [b]special resin[/b] called [b]copal[/b], which was extracted from one of two kinds of [b]busera trees[/b]. This resin was burned in small [b]incense burners[/b], which came in many different shapes, the most common ones having an elongated shape that ended with a [b]circle [/b]at the center for depositing the copal.

The chronicles tell about the general uses for copal, in public, domestic and private ceremonies for [b]commoners as well as nobles[/b].

The [b]tlamacazque [/b]offered the copal smoke directing it towards the [b]four cardinal points[/b], towards the [b]Sun [/b]and finally towards the image of a [b]deity[/b], with the purpose of linking men and gods, so the latter would favor the former. 

[b]This practice survived [/b]the Spanish conquest, as the use of copal is still present in many indigenous festivities of modern-day Mexico.

This image shows a tlamacazque, with his body painted black, carrying a bag containing copal, and an incense burner, which is based on those found in a massive offering of burners at the[b] Greater Temple[/b] in Mexico’s City.

[h3]Have you ever enjoyed the fragrant smell of copal?[/h3]

notes.title: Noble woman from Tulum
notes.content:
The Mayan noblewoman stood out for her intricate [b]jade ornaments[/b], fine clothes, the scarification [b]scars [/b]over her face and the use of complex[b] body paint[/b].

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/1af2fd42965158cb21d3f34adb35aff6062ffaad.jpg[/img]

In this WIP images you can appreciate a noblewoman in the coastal city of [b]Tulum[/b], notable for her sarong, a straight dress that leaves the shoulders bare, decored with [b]Mayan calendar symbols[/b]. She also wears ostentatious jade earrings inspired by those found on the mask of[b] King Pakal [/b]of Palenque and her body shows paintings as indicated in the texts of Fray Diego de Landa on his book [i]Relaciones de la Cosas de Yucatan[/i].

We seek to combine [b]reality with fiction[/b] in our designs, but keeping the dignity of a culture that continues to this day, and whose women are the source of its[b] resistance and permanence[/b] through the centuries.

notes.title: Coyote Warriors
notes.content:
Did you know that [b]Coyote warriors[/b] existed both with the Mexica and the Tlaxcalans?

The Coyote warrior appears numerous times in the History of Tlaxcala, participating on the side of the Mexica, as well as the Tlaxcalan. It also appears in Mixtec codices and in Teotihuacan murals. 

It was a creature of a [b]carnivorous nature and great libido[/b], and was associated with the immutable cycle of regeneration and death, the base of the Mesoamerican cosmovision; so it is not surprising that it sought to have its own power and strength, just as it was for the eagle and jaguar warriors.

The coyote was so important that the name of [b]Nezahualcoyotl[/b], an extraordinary character in Mesoamerican history (a poet, reformer, warrior and lover) means “[b]fasting coyote[/b]”.

This is why for this WIP we present a coyote warrior, in this case, a [b]fire coyote[/b], represented in the first memoirs. We based its shield on one of the few Mesoamerican shields that have survived to this day, besides adding multicolored plumage, representing the [b]noble background [/b]of the character.

notes.title: Spanish soldiers' equipment
notes.content:
[i]Mictlan [/i]is set in Mesoamerica, during the 16th century, in the early days of the [b]expedition of Cortes[/b]. Therefore, our academic team and our very talented conceptual artists have tried to [b]reconstruct [/b]with chronicles, studies and archaeological traces the history of the time, including the[b] first members [/b]of Hernan Cortes' company.

The soldiers of the 16th century were equipped with the [b]latest tools and weapons[/b], with the introduction of [b]firearms[/b], therefore battle strategies were gradually changing. Still, [b]other weapons [/b]also proved to be very useful, the best example being the sword, spear, halberd and crossbow.

According to [b]Lopez de Gomara's chronicle[/b], the Spaniards were mostly armed with swords and daggers, in accordance with the data collected by Sahagún and Bernal Díaz del Castillo's own account. 

As for their [b]clothing[/b], it varied according to their socioeconomic condition, as some were able to afford iron breastplates, while others would be left with simpler protections.

notes.title: The Wise Elder
notes.content:
[b]Old age [/b]was a very important stage for pre-Hispanic cultures, it was believed that the elderly were those who knew the [b]truth[/b] and could transmit it to those around them.

The old men were considered wise, with incredible mental strength. Many times, they fulfilled the role of [b]advisers and guides[/b] in celebrations and rituals, always knowing the appropriate moment to act or not to act.

With all references we studied, our artists were inspired to create this concept art of an [b]Elder Sage[/b], a character with a certain mastery over nature and time.

He carries a plume of feathers and natural fibers, he also wears a cloth and fur cloak matching with his [i]maxtlatl[/i], both with wooden and leather finishes. His staff ends with a deer antler.

The Elder Sage can teach the players [b]important lessons[/b] inside the universe of [i]Mictlan[/i], help you to [b]summon gods[/b], reveal secrets about nahual transformation and about your journey to the underworld.

notes.title: Battles between Spaniards and indigenous people
notes.content:
Spaniards and indigenous people had various [b]confrontations [/b]throughout the conquest period, in the different regions of Latin America.

In the case of Mesoamerica, diplomatic relations were always the first battlefields, since the support from indigenous subjects of the triple alliance was essential for the fall of the Mexica culture.

In this concept art shows a fight presenting various elements that set the tone of the [b]clashes between Spaniards and indigenous people[/b], including new tools such as horses and metal protections.
[b]
Terrible battles[/b] unfolded under the wing of the conquest and you as a player will be able to relive some of them in the adventure that awaits you in [i]Mictlan: An Ancient Mythical Tale[/i].

notes.content:
As you have seen in [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/2870472829289484594]our previous posts[/url], Mexica priests dressed in very simple clothes for their daily chores, using [i]maxtla [/i](loincloth) and [i]xicollis [/i](nightgowns), reserving the extravagant ornaments for the festivities to celebrate deities. 

For this [b]priest of Mictlantecuhtli [/b]we opted for a more fantastic approach, although based on our previous studies of pre-Hispanic clothing and iconography: as you know by now, in [i]Mictlan [/i]we always strive for a balance between fantasy and historical accuracy.

notes.title: Facial animations
notes.content:
We are currently testing numerous [b]facial animation techniques[/b] with a small group of voice actors.

What you see here is all done [b]manually[/b], adjusting each muscle of the face, moving it accordingly to the expressions and speech of the dialogue. 

Another technique we are testing is [b]full performance capture[/b], which means we can record body and face expressions as well as audio in real-time, this method is extremely [b]difficult and costly[/b] so, until we launch our [url=https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/mictlanthegame/micltan-the-video-game?ref=clipboard-prelaunch]Kickstarter campaign[/url], we can only proceed to create most of the face animations manually. 

These are just [b]experiments[/b], we're constantly trying to achieve better results in order to arrive to our [b]finalized version [/b]of the game in the future years. 

Anyway, we're more than happy with our work so far, what do you think?

notes.title: Aztec buildings repurposed by another faith
notes.content:
Did you know that when the Spanish conquistadors conquered Tenochtitlan in 1521, they immediately destroyed one of the [b]most important temples[/b] in the city to make room for what would become the principal [b]Christian church[/b] in the capital of New Spain? 

This became a common practice, and over 68 churches [b]were built over[/b] prehispanic buildings that had sacred meaning to the indigenous people.

notes.title: The Jaguar Warlock
notes.content:
The jaguar was one of the most [b]worshipped beings[/b], not only by the Mexica but also by almost all of the Mesoamerica people. It was said that those who were born on the day of "océlotl" would be the best at war, that they would show their courage and strength.

It is also claimed that there were people who were capable of transforming into the [b]powerful felines[/b], who could acquire superhuman strength and knowledge.

With this inspiration and stories in mind, our artists have created this fantastic concept of the [b]Jaguar Warlock[/b], a character who expresses all of his power through the fur clothing with the characteristic spotted design of the jaguar, but who also has a mystical aura, like the jaguar himself, [b]lord of all animals[/b].

We have not yet defined his powers or abilities, but perhaps you, community of [i]Mictlán [/i]can help us. What else would you like to see about this character?

notes.title: Miquiztetl #4
notes.content:
The cruel [b]Miquiztetl [/b]was a [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/partnerevents/preview/4941001585200991435]deity from the underworld [/url]who tried to stop the dead from overcoming the trials of the nine regions. Their journey lasted 4 years, before arriving in Mictlán.

A skillful warrior and the [b]twin sister of the God of Dreams[/b], she attacked those who descended into the world of the dead and terrified them with her fierce and skeletal body. She attacked with her weapons and made them fall into different [b]traps [/b]that they had to overcome, before going through the nine levels that blocked their access to Mictlan.

After a long journey through the underground regions, the dead had to [b]get rid of their fears[/b], avoid traps, and tricks by Miquiztetl, to prove that they were capable of [b]freeing their Tonalli (soul) [/b]from all the burdens or flaws. They would finally arrive in front of the[b] lord and mistress of death[/b]: Mictlantecuhtli and Mictlancíhuatl, rulers of the underworld, who would allow the dead to leave behind all the pain that they had carried during their whole lives and then finally resting.

notes.title: Mayan women: a study
notes.content:
Did you know that [b]Mayan women[/b] liked perfume and a daily bath with cold water?

In [i]Yucatan at the Time of the Spanish Encounter[/i] by Fray Diego de Landa, chapter XXXI mentions the following about the cosmetics and clothing of Mayan women:

[quote]Their noses were pierced through the small square that divides the windows in the middle to put an amber stone in the hole and had it as an ornament.
They pierced their ears to put on earrings in the same way of their husbands; carved their body from the waist up, except for the breasts.

The Indian women of the provinces of Bacalar and Campeche dressed very modestly. The breasts were covered by tying the clothes under the armpits using a folded blanket. All the others did not wear any clothing other than a long and wide jacket open on both sides.[/quote]

O the basis of the descriptions and reconstructions from the murals, codex vessels and clay figures by Daniel Parada (Aka Zotz), we shaped our own study of what a[b] noble and commoner woman of Yucatan[/b] would look like during the period of the Spanish conquest. Moving away from the stereotypes present in Apocalypto, seeking a respectful balance between[b] historical authenticity and fantasy[/b].

What do you think?

notes.title: Codex collection
notes.content:
As with any good video game inspired by history, in [i]Mictlán: An Ancient Mythical Tale[/i] you will be able to find [b]hundreds [/b]of facts and information about the historic time and place that the game is inspired by.

Every landscape, character and artifact that you find will be registered as your own [b]codex[/b], which you will be able to access any time you want and learn a bit more about them.

For example, every [b]weapon [/b]you add to your collection will have a description with the name’s origin, how it was made and of which materials. 
You will also be able to rotate it on its axles so you can appreciate not only the [b]beauty of the original handicraft[/b] but also the [b]amazing work[/b] of our developers, from our concept artists to our 3D modelers.

notes.title: Pentamuti
notes.content:
Hello [i]Mictlan [/i]fans!

What character would you like to see represented in [i]Mictlan [/i]from one of the many [b]Mexican pre-Hispanic cultures[/b]?

Our intent is to give[b] visibility and representation [/b]in our game to the great civilizations that existed throughout Mexico.

In this concept art, you can see the [b]Pentamuti[/b], or Purépecha or Tarascan priest, the person responsible for watching over the Cuerauaperi cult, mother goddess of the Purepecha culture.

As you can see, the character wears a richly decorated [i]xicolli [/i]or nightgown, accompanied by [b]ornaments [/b]of bronze and gold, since the Purépecha were renowned [b]goldsmiths [/b]who worked metals, especially copper, and their knowledge gave them an advantage over their Mexican rivals. This character also wears a [b]funerary mask[/b], possibly for a mortuary ritual. Hanging behind him, a huge dry gourd that serves either to store water for libations in honor of the gods, or as a deposit of medicinal powders used to heal the sick.

What do you think?

notes.title: Terrible omens
notes.content:
Omens and divinations were part of[b] Mexica mysticism[/b], so it is not surprising that the wise men and Tlatoanis interpreted the strange [b]signs [/b]that appeared before the conquest of Tenochtitlán as signals sent by the gods, a warning about [b]the end of an era[/b] and of the cyclical battle between the gods.

The passing of a [b]comet[/b], the [b]lightning [/b]strike at the Xiuhtecuhtli temple, the sudden [b]fire [/b]of the Templo Mayor, the appearance of a "[b]weeping woman[/b]" in the streets, crying out in the night, warning her "children" to flee.

The final omen was when a [b]two-headed monster[/b] was discovered in the city of Tenochtitlan.

All the omens revealed the [b]uncertainty of the future [/b]of the Mexica nation in the face of fate. 
[i]A grim future indeed.[/i]

notes.title: Yohualtepoztli
notes.content:
This is the story of one of the most [b]frightening beings[/b] in Tenochtitlan: it exists to [b]torment nocturnal travelers[/b], a beast that appears to the ones who dare to walk alone at night. 

A humanoid creature, that has no head. Its chest is wide open: a revolting, bloody cavity displaying its [b]heart[/b], trapped in the ribcage.

[i]Thud. Thud. Thud. [/i]
You'll hear it coming, like an [b]axe [/b]being driven into wood.
That's where the name of the [b]Yohualtepoztli [/b]comes from: [i]yohualli[/i], “night”, and [i]tepoztli[/i], “axe”.

Faced with this creature, there's little you can to: either [b]flee [/b]or try to [b]rip its heart off its chest[/b].

So, [i]what will it be?[/i]

notes.title: The power of Unreal Engine 5
notes.content:
A couple months back, we upgraded to [b]Unreal Engine 5[/b], which gives us the possibility of working with [b]photogrammetric scanned assets[/b], and keeping the same level of graphics. Millions of un-optimized polygons are the[b] dream [/b]that any developer could ever dream of.

To be able to deliver a world using the latest technology in terms of graphics, our awesome team is working on the details of the [b]micro-world[/b] inside the videogame.

We are working with many groups in Mexico to [b]scan jungles[/b], [b]mountains[/b], [b]plants[/b], [b]rocks[/b], and even the smallest details in the environment, to give that touch of [b]realism [/b]never seen before in LATAM.
Our dream is to create the first open-world videogame based on [b]pre-Hispanic cultures[/b]. To accomplish this, we are learning, investigating and researching to [b]make this dream a reality[/b].

notes.title: Sisimite #2
notes.content:
Remember the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/2992060508099033138]concept art[/url] we shared about the [b]sisimite[/b]? 

A truly savage creature which is slowly coming to life thanks to the work of our incredible art team: 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/b7e61c153fb3b0a52b72884b2db4bd477a41faa8.jpg[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/594fa235dc7a72eac5591bc8b3e04616c61f717a.jpg[/img]

This ape-like creature, with disturbing backward-facing feet, is mistakenly known by some people as the “[b]Mexican Bigfoot[/b]”. It's actually a creature from the legends in Honduras, Guatemala, Belize, Nicaragua and El Salvador.

It dwells in hidden caves in the Central American [b]high mountains[/b], and all the stories about it describe the sisimite as a [b]morally ambivalent creature[/b]. On one hand, it is an[b] herbivore [/b]that feeds on wild fruits and protects small animals from human hunters and fishermen. On the other hand, it captures women and takes them to the caves, forcing them to give birth to ape-men.

Despite its scary appearance, you'll be glad to know that the sisimite has[b] two elemental weaknesses[/b]: water and fire. 

[b]Picture this[/b]: you are backtracking a set of four-fingered footprints leading to the mountain; there, you find the sisimite’s lair, and you bravely chase it away (or even defeat it!) exploiting its elemental weaknesses, finally reaching your objective: a cave that will grant you access to the underworld.

This is just an idea, but… how do you imagine your own encounter with the sisimite in the open world of [i]Mictlan[/i]?

notes.title: How we're including the Nahual in Mictlan
notes.content:
The legends of the [b]nahual [/b]in Mexico have deep roots in [b]magical events [/b]and folklore.

These mythical beings are [b]guardian-spirits[/b] intimately linked to their humans, who feel a mix of fear and admiration before their extraordinary powers.

Nahual is believed to reside in an [b]animal[/b], such as a deer, jaguar, or bird. Others believe the nagual is the animal into which certain [b]powerful men[/b] can transform themselves, acquiring the animal's unbelievable skills (we've talked about the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3005569403402945591]Nahual kids[/url] before).

🔥 In [i]Mictlan[/i], we've been working really hard to design a [b]special dynamic[/b] in which the characters can contact their nahual (spiritual companion) by two different methods.

🐆 They can make an [b]invocation[/b] to let these creatures manifest themselves in the physical world as [b]allies [/b]in battle and as an aid to discover [b]secret locations[/b]. 

🐦 We also thought about the idea of letting the player [b]become one with their nahual[/b], transforming themself into powerful animals with a [b]unique set of abilities[/b].

[h3]What do you think? Would you call you nahual in the game? Would you prefer transforming yourself into one? 

We would really appreciate [b]your feedback[/b] about this. 
Let us know what you think in the comments![/h3]

notes.title: Huehuecoyotl #2
notes.content:
Its [b]howls [/b]have been deaf for centuries, its songs and music have been nothing more than just [b]empty echoes[/b], desperate to be heard [b]once more[/b].

In [i]Mictlan [/i]you will be able to hear the nocturnal howls of [b]Huehuecoyotl[/b], the god of the arts, music and dance. ([url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3029213935088016668]We showed you the concept art of this character in this post![/url])

Its name is derived from Nahuatl and means "[b]Old Coyote[/b]", as it is represented as a virile man with the face of a coyote. A warrior and [b]sower of discord[/b] among men, Huehuecoyotl was also described as a [i]malsin [/i](that is, a gossiper).

Huehuecoyotl is considered a god of [b]good luck[/b], based on the fact that he is the one who represents the limit between good and evil. He [b]balances [/b]the old and the new, the mundane and the spiritual, the youth and the old, the male and the female, since he has the ability to [b]change gende[/b]r. It is also characterized by [b]lust[/b] and [b]carnal desire[/b], giving way to the erotic dimension of the ancient Mexicas.

notes.title: Tlacamexquimilli
notes.content:
[b]Tlacamexquimilli[/b]: Bulk of Ashes

When a Mexica died from natural causes, the [b]body was wrapped[/b] in a fetal position inside of a rucksack, along with different elements that they would need in [b]their journey to [i]Mictlan[/i][/b].

But, apparently, some of them [b]did not make it [/b]to that point, and they would appear as “[b]spirits[/b]”, roaming the roads and streets. They would take the form of a [b]bulk of ashes[/b] or of a [b]shrouded corpse[/b], they could have many heads or legs, or resemble a[b] shapeless mass[/b], full of eyes and sharp teeth, wandering in the night to scare the living.

On many occasions, people would [b]die from fear[/b] caused by ghosts.

Some said that this was actually [b]a trick from Tezcatlipoc[/b]a to test the warriors. If they were brave, he would reward them with a [b]symbolic gift[/b]; but if they were cowards, they would[b] surely die[/b] on the battlefield or from diseases. 

These are some pieces from our designers, they still are in progress [b]#WIP[/b].

[h3]Which one do you find more terrifying?[/h3]

notes.title: Cuauhtemoc
notes.content:
[b]Cuauhtemoc[/b], the [i]descending eagle[/i]. 

What a prophetic name for such a [b]heroic and tragic figure[/b] in the history of Mexico! 

He did not inherit a flourishing empire like Moctezuma II, but one fragmented by the European invasion. As the [b]military leader[/b] of the Mexica, he fought for the survival of his people, [b]fortifying the city of Tenochtitlan[/b] and preparing his people for a war without truce, a war that would culminate in the [b]destruction[/b] of one of the most impressive cities in pre-Hispanic America.

How to do justice to [b]such a remarkable figure[/b]? 

In the [b]concept art[/b] we created, we decided not to show Cuauhtemoc in the typical attire of his rank, but fighting like a [i]macehual [/i]warrior. Of course, he's wearing some emblems that represent the [b]important position[/b] he held, but the general [b]modest attire[/b] represents the lack of resources and the [b]suffering of the besieged city[/b] that he tried to defend so bravely. At the same time, Cuauhtemoc's [b]defiant pose[/b] reminds us of his legendary [b]stoicism and courage[/b], ready to sacrifice himself for his people, to safeguard a world that was doomed, but that he refused to let go without a [b]fierce fight[/b]. 

[h3]Which one of these variations is your favorite? 

Let us know in the comments![/h3]

notes.title: Tarascan warrior
notes.content:
Hello, dear followers of [i]Mictlan[/i]! 

Today we want to show you some concept art pieces related to the [b]Michoacan region[/b].

The West of Mexico is still an [b]enigma [/b]for archaeologists: the migratory flow of the region has not yet been precisely determined, but the archaeological evidence discovered so far speaks of contacts from time immemorial with the [b]Andean area[/b], reflected in the ceramics and lithics found in the Tombs of the [b]Colima region[/b].

That is why, in order to represent the [b]Tarascan warrior[/b], we took into account the relations of [b]Michoacan [/b](a document created by the Franciscan Fray Jerónimo de Alcalá), which illustrates in details the customs and beliefs of the people of the Michoacan region, as well as their history during the [b]Spanish conquest[/b].

We also refer to some [b]sculptures [/b]found in the Colima region that represent warriors from that area, who fought against the Tarascans and who, in turn, served as their mercenaries in the so-called "[b]saltpeter wars[/b]"

This WIP was made by [b]MarioRicoArt[/b]. If you want to know more about his work, visit his [url=https://www.marioricoart.com/]website[/url].

notes.title: Palace of Moctezuma II
notes.content:
In this new piece of concept art, we want to show the facade of the [b]palace of Moctezuma II[/b], an architectural complex that the Tlatoani ordered to be built as a residence and seat of[b] government of the city of Tenochtitlan[/b], thus replacing the old palace of Axayacatl and thereby giving life to a glorious government that would [b]end abruptly[/b] after the arrival of the Spanish conquistadores to Mesoamerica.

The chroniclers of the time, such as Bernal Díaz del Castillo's, described in detail the palace of Moctezuma II. In the words of [b]Hernán Cortés[/b]:

[quote]He had his lodgings within the city, such and so wonderful, that it seemed almost impossible to tell the goodness and greatness of them. Therefore, I won’t be able to express something about them, more than that in Spain there is no one similar.[/quote]

Given that the [b]archaeological evidence is scarce[/b] since the Moctezuma palace lies buried in the metropolitan area of ​​Mexico City and that the descriptions of [b]Fray Bernardino de Sahagún [/b]would be written several years after the destruction of Tenochtitlan, we took [b]some artistic liberties[/b], supported by Mexica architectural remains of the time, and speculation of how the great palace of Moctezuma II could have been.

[h3]What do you think of this WIP?[/h3]

notes.title: The Great Tenochtitlan #2
notes.content:
Here is another update about the [b]biggest and most advanced city[/b] in the 15th century. That's right, we're talking about [b]Tenochtitlan[/b]!

If you missed the [b]previous posts[/b] about it, here they are: [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/2969545680704939381]#1[/url], [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/2969546585728032228]#2[/url] 

The city had a wonderful and well-planned[b] tangle of streets[/b] and canals that gave it a mystical (and functional) look.
The streets of Tenochtitlan had sidewalks of rammed earth* for human transit, and some of them had adjacent [b]canals [/b]for the transit of canoes that transported and commercialized a lot of different products.

The first [b]main street[/b] (and the most used for commercial purposes) was [b]Tlalpan[/b], built by the Xochimilcas as an act of tribute to the Mexica; it started in Xochimilco and ended in Tenochtitlan.

notes.content:
[b]You[/b]. An [b]NPC [/b]in [i]Mictlan[/i]. Interacting with the players.

Do you want to be [b]immortalized [/b]in a video game?

Each NPC will have a different[b] cinematic animation[/b] for their purchase sequences, making it [b]unique [/b]in the entire open world of [i]Mictlan[/i], something never seen before in Latin America.

Remember that the [b]Pochtecas [/b]traded with different types of merchandise and materials. 

Would you like your NPC to trade only [b]rare materials[/b] like turquoise, obsidian, quetzal feathers and furs?

Or would you rather be a merchant of [b]mystical plants[/b] like mushrooms, peyotes, toadskin and tobacco?

The Pochtecas had a [b]complex system of hierarchies[/b] that depended on the characteristics of the merchant and their military or nobility alliances. The most important ones were the [b]Teucnehnenqueh [/b]or "great merchants", those who made deals with the nobility.

notes.title: The Great Tenochtitlan
notes.content:
Today we present to you the [b]incredible work[/b] that our 3D artists, lead by our talented artist [b]Josharts3d[/b], are doing in recreating the[b] Great Tenochtitlan[/b].

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/08d9295b1a766b1abe33ebdbd5103a26464d8508.jpg[/img]

The faithful recreation of this place will be of utmost importance since Tenochtitlan was [b]the center of the Aztec universe[/b].
Just in its [b]Great Plaza [/b]were over [b]80 buildings[/b] between temples, altars, warrior rooms, the Calmecac, palaces and other structures.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/518e3b64da03b4d3bdef8b16841673841c86987c.jpg[/img]

[b]The residences of the nobility [/b]and [b]administrative buildings[/b] were organized around squares or open spaces, connected by roads and canals. Artisans and peasants organized themselves into neighborhoods or [i]Calpullis[/i]. According to Roger Bartra's calculations, the population was around [b]700,000[/b].

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/3b3fd5913e057e436637bb4397c5d8e2be14aad5.jpg[/img]

This data [b]is all the more impressive[/b] when thinking about the fact that the city was founded on an [b]islet [/b]in Lake Texcoco, and that the Aztecs built [b]artificial islands [/b]as villages that, as the settlement expanded, were eventually [b]integrated into the city[/b].

notes.title: The coastal city of Tulum
notes.content:
Today we proudly present to you some images (WIP) of a level dedicated to one of the [b]most powerful coastal settlements[/b] in the late Postclassic period, the great walled city of the Caribbean: [b]Tulum[/b]. 

Known in the 16th century as [b]Zamá [/b](which means “[b]dawn[/b]”), the site of Tulum was one of the most important centers of exchange on the sea that connected the Gulf of Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America. It was a [b]seaport[/b], trading mainly in turquoise and jade.

The hard work of our [b]3D department[/b] resulted in an artistic reconstruction of the main architectural complexes in the city, so that you can [b]explore the castle[/b], the Temple of Frescoes, the Temple of the Falling God, and the palaces and altars all around the [b]archaeological zone[/b]. 

[i]Note[/i]:

notes.title: The challenges behind Mictlan
notes.content:
It is not easy to develop a video game such as [i]Mictlan[/i]. 

The[b] level of hyperrealism [/b]that we have set to achieve takes a lot of work and a talented team. It all starts with [b]historiographic research[/b], then our artists create[b] concept art[/b], which finally reaches the capable hands of our [b]3D modelers[/b]. They are the ones who, at a high level of [b]digital craftsmanship[/b], build everything that you will admire in [i]Mictlan[/i]: buildings, diverse biomes, weapons, animals and, of course, characters.

We are an [b]independent studio[/b], so we have to use a public software. Fortunately, [b]Unreal Engine [/b]gives our artists the possibility to accomplish amazing things and achieve a level of detail and quality that we plan to offer to our players.

But it is not just about the tools: it is the talent and the [b]heart of our team[/b], mostly Mexican people, which makes [i]Mictlan [/i]a project that will surpass everything that has been done among video games in Latin America to this day. 

[b]Your help[/b], the help of [b]our community[/b] is fundamental to achieve this dream and shift the paradigms for a lot of Latin American creators.

notes.title: Mexico-Tenochtitlan causeways
notes.content:
Greetings, dear [i]Mictlan [/i]fans!

Today, we will talk about the [b]Mexico-Tenochtitlan causeways[/b].

Roads, unlike the numerous canals that crossed the city, had been designed with the purpose of speeding up the[b] traffic of people[/b] inside and outside the city, as well as the [b]circulation of goods[/b] that could not travel by lake. These causeways had a [b]considerable length[/b], up to 20 meters, a [b]feat of engineering[/b] achieved in ancient Mexico.

There were [b]four main roads[/b] in the city. 
[i]Iztapalapa [/i]was the busiest; it faced south and connected the city with the towns of Coyoacan, Xochimilco and Chalco. [i]Tacuba [/i]led to the west. Towards the north, a minor one led to a canal named Tezontlali, which was connected to Tepeyac; and finally, [i]Tepeyac [/i] was connected to a large pier that gave access to the kingdom of Texcoco.

In [i]Mictlan[/i], we want [b]the players to travel[/b] these important routes and immerse themselves in the [b]daily life[/b] of this mythical city.

Note: This is not the final render, you will enjoy the finished version of Tenochtitlan at the end of 2024 - 2025

notes.title: Miquiztetl
notes.content:
The cruel [b]Miquiztetl[/b] was a deity from the underworld who tried to stop the dead from overcoming the trials of the nine regions. When people died, they had to travel for 4 years, before arriving to [i]Mictlán[/i].

A skillful warrior and twin sister of the [b]God of Dreams[/b], she attacked those who descended to the world of the dead and [b]terrified them[/b] with her fierce and skeletal body. She attacked with her weapons and made them fall into different [b]traps [/b]that the dead had to overcome, before going through the nine levels that blocked their access to [i]Mictlan[/i].

After a long journey through the underground regions, the dead had to rid of their [b]fears[/b], traps, and tricks of Miquiztetl, to prove that they were capable of freeing their [i]Tonalli [/i]([b]soul[/b]) from all the life burdens.

They finally arrived in front of the [b]lord and mistress of death[/b]: Mictlantecuhtli and Mictlancíhuatl, rulers of the underworld, who allowed the souls to leave behind all the pain that they had carried during their lives, in order to finally [b]rest in peace[/b].

notes.title: Beauty standards in the pre-Hispanic world
notes.content:
There were many beauty standards in the pre-Hispanic world, when the[b] cult of the body [/b]was central. 

As we've [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1411900/view/3026951542954716803]discussed before in this post[/url], the ancient populations considered the human body as a small representation of the cosmo and used the body as a "[b]canvas[/b]" to achieve the ideal beauty.  
They [b]altered [/b]their physical appearance in many ways, such as body paint, tattoos, jewelry: all of this represented an expression of [b]cultural identity[/b] and [b]social belonging[/b].

[b]Scarification [/b]was another method used by ancient civilizations to signify important events in one's life, as well as to symbolize differing class distinctions. This process consisted of multiple [b]skin perforations[/b], followed by stuffing the wound with some kind of irritating substance, such as small stones, dirt or ashes. This process led to several [b]scars [/b]with different textures, forming [b]complex patterns[/b].

The evidence these practices (tattooing, scarification, and body paint) among the Maya comes from [b]iconographic images[/b] such as pottery and murals, artifacts such as tools and vessels used for storing pigment and anthropomorphic sculptures.

notes.title: Teotihuacan
notes.content:
Among the archeological sites found in Mexico that are open to the public, [b]Teotihuacan [/b]is one of the most visited by tourists from all over the world, even more than Chichen Itza and Monte Alban. 

It is usual, among the people who visit Mexico City for their first time, to take some pictures at the top of the [b]Pyramid of the Sun[/b], as a token to remember the tiring trek up the dozens of very small and steep stairs, in order to “[b]recharge with positive energy[/b]”.

Although some of these popular beliefs derive from recent movements such as [i]the new age[/i], it is true that you can feel a [b]mystic and enigmatic presence[/b] when walking through the historical roads of the site, between the elite houses of the ancient Teotihuacan society. 

And it is not just us that perceive this mysterious feeling: half a millennium ago, the Mexica, trying to understand how such a [b]grand and majestic city [/b]ended up being abandoned, decided to entitle it as “the [b]City of Gods[/b]” and to establish it as the origin of the[b] Fifth Sun[/b], so that it effectively became the birthplace of the last era of the world as we know it.

Beyond myths and tales, it is actually proven that, in order to build it, its architects observed the position of the [b]celestial bodies[/b], taking into consideration the calendar in order to mark ritual and agricultural seasons. 

Besides, we can’t overlook the strange[b] coincidences[/b] with the construction of the Pyramid of Cheops in Egypt: they have [b]striking architectural similarities[/b], even if built by two completely unrelated societies.

What do you expect to find when you play [i]Mictlan [/i]and go visit Teotihuacan? 
Do you have any pictures of you in this enigmatic city? Share in the comments [url=https://www.facebook.com/mictlanthegame/posts/291813155977356]to this post[/url]!

notes.title: Macehuales
notes.content:
Greetings, [i]Mictlan [/i]community!

Today we will talk about the [i]macehuales[/i]: the base of Mexica society.

Aztec society was strictly [b]hierarchical[/b], divided into clearly defined classes so that individuals would have remained in the social group of their immediate family throughout their lives.

The macehuales were by far the[b] largest section [/b]of Aztec society, they were the ones who cultivated the land, those who paid the taxes and reinforced the size of the army.

Aside from the commoner-warriors, the macehual class was further [b]differentiated [/b]into class levels. Certain occupations were considered to have [b]higher prestige[/b] than others (such as merchants, goldsmiths, and featherworkers). In general, compared with rural farming, all [b]urban [/b]occupations were assigned higher status.

Macehuales had a [b]hard [/b]and [b]humble life[/b], always working long hours to get by.

In this concept art you can see a young macehual with a [i]mecapal[/i], a container which was widely used in pre-Hispanic times to transport [b]all kinds of goods[/b], goods which would surely be exchanged in the [i]tianguis[/i] (open-air market) of Tlatelolco.
We also drew the young boy with a [i]coa[/i], a [b]digging tool [/b]that was used for farming and at the time, also as an improvised weapon.

notes.title: Huitzilopochtli
notes.content:
[b]Huitzilopochtli[/b], the god of war and of the sun, representing the mythical battle of [b]light against the darkness[/b]. A mighty and powerful god, whose strength derives from the [b]vital force[/b] of those who sacrificed themselves to him, from the [b]blood of the hearts[/b] that were offered to him.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/6cef8e62da38c6b013f44b233c1a74d7c72ce787.jpg[/img]

In these pictures, we want to show you one of the first versions of the Aztec god we created for [i]Micltan[/i]. We took the liberty of mixing the [b]historical [/b]codices with a [b]fantasy [/b]look suitable to represent this powerful figure.

notes.title: Atlatl
notes.content:
Commonly known as a spear-thrower, the [b]Atlatl [/b]is, without a doubt, a [b]deadly weapon[/b]. 

This powerful weapon allowed warriors to throw spears from a great distance with deadly [b]force and speed[/b], easily piercing through any armor or enemy.

The weapon has an elongated body that ends in a [b]hook [/b]where the darts are placed, and it also possesses a handle with two perforations for a strong finger [b]grip[/b]. 
Capable of reaching a speed of[b] 130 km/h [/b](80 mph), [b]darts [/b]made of wood, flint, teeth, bone or obsidian. They were able to pierce the flesh and incapacitate an enemy [b]within seconds[/b]. 

In Mesoamerica, the Atlatl earned its fair place as a symbol of[b] war[/b], [b]power [/b]and [b]greatness[/b]. 
It became a must during the classic era wars. It was so important that in the temple of Jaguars, in Chichen Itza, almost [b]180 different soldiers [/b]were represented holding this particular weapon. 

[h3]Will you use the Atlatl in Mictlan? Or do you prefer melee weapons? 
Let us know in the comments! [/h3]

notes.title: Spanish Soldiers
notes.content:
It is a [b]popular myth[/b] that the military efforts made by the Conquistadores were led by professional armies financed entirely by the Spanish crown while, actually, the exploration and conquest were carried out by [b]companies [/b]that were always [b]private [/b]in nature, which had to have the consent of the Crown.

in this concept art we show a few [b]Castilian warriors[/b], who stand out for their clothing and weapons; it is a very basic attire, since they only had the necessary equipment for a [b]hand-to-hand confrontation[/b]: a metal breatplate, a leather gown, which at the time were replaced by the padded armor known as [i]Ichcahuipilli[/i], since it was much more comfortable and protected the soldiers from arrows more efficiently.

During our studies, we realized that the morion helmet was not used by the Castilians in their initial expeditions to the Mexican territory, so we proceeded to study other styles of helmet used during the war; we also added the [b]adarga shield[/b], widely used in the Iberian Peninsula due to influence of the Berber people during the Caliphate period, until the Reconquest, and its use is documented in in documents such as the [i]Lienzo de Tlaxcala[/i].

notes.title: Nahual Kids #2
notes.content:
According to the different traditions of Mesoamerican cultures, it is believed that the first creature to cross over the ashes spread before a newborn baby becomes that child’s [b]nahual[/b], a [b]guardian spirit[/b]. 

Every newborn has their own personal guardian, depending on their day of birth. A spirit that watches over them and [b]protects them[/b]. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/4b82f147c64c048e6df99f5120982c0d7f12bad5.jpg[/img]

Kids can acquire [b]gifts [/b]and [b]special powers[/b] from their nahual, which can take the form of [b]various animals[/b] such as a jaguar, an eagle, a deer, or a snake (among others). 

The gifts can be granted but also removed and, if not handled well, they can [b]take hold of the will [/b]of a young person in the teenage years. That's why every Nagual kid has to learn to control and master their powers otherwise their entire existence is on the line.

In [i]Mictlan[/i], you will encounter these characters who can become your [b]greatest allies[/b]... or your [b]worst nightmare[/b].

notes.title: Huehuecoyotl
notes.content:
The Aztec god of poetry, music, dance, and mischief: [b]Huehuecoyotl[/b], the "Old Coyote", enters the pantheon of [i]Mictlan[/i]'s gods.

This very [b]unique-looking god[/b] is usually represented wearing garments made of "olive" shells and copper bells on arms and legs, which are associated with wind and music. He also has golden beads that fall from his hand as pictured in [i]Codex Borgia[/i]. 

In Aztec culture, coyotes were a symbol of [b]cunning [/b]and [b]worldly wisdom[/b], Huehuecoyotl is also associated with [b]worldly desires [/b]and [b]unbridled sexuality[/b]: he is one of those gods considered as a combination between good and evil.

[b]Alex Loera [/b]is the talented artist in our team who designed these versions of Huehuecoyotl.

notes.title: Tzizimine
notes.content:
The mythical world of [i]Mictlan [/i]is wide and it hides the scariest deities, so terrifying that they could not be imagined... because we've drawn them for you! 

Here we present to you the [b]Tzizimine[/b], women-like creatures, with rotten, decaying flesh which reveal the skeleton underneath, with clawed hands and feet, wearing ornaments made of [b]skull necklaces[/b] and[b] human hearts[/b].

The Tzizimine are [b]nocturnal deities[/b] whose purpose was to devour human beings at the end of the Fifth Sun. They would descend from the sky at night and stalk the little kids to kidnap them. They would also appear in the [b]eclipses [/b]to eat the sun and swallow the entire humanity.

Our visual artist [b]Sergio Vázquez Heredia[/b] has created different versions of these creatures: from [b]beautiful women[/b] who wait for travelers at the crossroads, to rotten and [b]hungry creatures[/b].

notes.title: Tenochtitlan
notes.content:
[b]Tenochtitlan[/b], the capital of the Aztec empire, was founded by the Aztec or Mexica people around 1325 C.E. According to [b]legend[/b], the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan after leaving their homeland of Aztlan at the direction of their god, [b]Huitzilopochtli[/b]. Huitzilopochtli instructed them to build their city in the location where they saw an[b] eagle perched on a cactus[/b] while eating a snake. 

This would be the signal that they had [b]found their home[/b].

We're bringing Tenochtitlan back to life in [i]Mictlan: An Ancient Mythical Tale[/i], so that you'll enjoy its bustling heart and street life, [b]wandering[/b] around, [b]interacting [/b]with the environment and with all the [b]people [/b]inhabiting the place.

After our [b]research phase[/b] involving articles, writings, stories, codices etc. we create every spot and building planning it out with careful consideration and with a great level of detail, guided by the [b]mood board[/b] precedently created to choose the right colors, shapes and details which help us give our creations a sense of [b]authenticity[/b].

[h3]Are you excited about the idea of walking around the great capital of the Aztec civilization?

Leave us a comment![/h3]

notes.title: The creative process behind the scenes
notes.content:
Here is a [b]sneak peek [/b]behind the curtains of the development process of [i]Mictlan: An Ancient Mythical Tale.[/i]

There is a [b]very long process[/b] behind every scene we intend to bring on the screen when our videogame will be finally ready. First of all, the idea of how the scene should be presented is conveyed through [b]concept art[/b], then a [b]mood board[/b] is created in order to communicate the "feel" of our idea and, according to it, lightening, colors and tones are defined.

This is only the first step, followed by a long process going through blocking, 3D recreation, ambiance, post-processing, animation, cameras, dialogues, cinematics, music, sound effects... [b]Everything has to be perfect[/b] in order to create the best videogame we can create, always keeping in mind the final look and feel we want to convey in [i]Mictlan[/i].

In today's post, we are sharing with you some of the [b]sketches [/b]that our amazing concept art team has created, along with a mood board which serves as a reference in this particular scene. 

[h3]What do these images communicate to you? Let us know in the comments![/h3]

notes.title: #TributoATonantzin
notes.content:
[h3]This week we want to celebrate all the extraordinary [b]Tonantzin[/b] in our lives![/h3]

In Nahuatl, the word “[i]Nantli[/i]” means "[b]mother[/b]", so the meaning of “[i]Tonantzin[/i]” is “[b]our beloved mother[/b]”, which was how the ancient Mexicas used to call the mother goddess: [b]Coatlicue[/b]. 

We want to celebrate all the women that have raised, educated and accompanied us in our lives. It doesn't matter if they are your biological mothers or not, your sisters, your mentors or your friends. 

📷[b]Take a picture[/b] with the woman in your life that inspires you, the one who has become your spiritual [i]Nantli[/i], and then [b]share it on your social media[/b] with the hashtags:

notes.title: Quinametzin
notes.content:
The [b]Quinametzin [/b] are the race of giants that inhabited Mexico in ancient times.

We are working on five different versions of these [b]mythical giants[/b], experimenting with various designs, very different from the first versions that we presented to you when we first started the development of [i]Mictlan[/i].

There are many [b]stories and myths[/b] in Mesoamerican cultures about these mythical creatures, So far, we have included in our game [b]three different versions[/b] of these giants, and we are also working on different types of mechanics and various body types: elongated Mayan skulls, tree-like creatures, giant orcs...

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/06096094bf6dc7e9b5cba89098ce5277f2f92b42.jpg[/img]

There are so many [b]Mesoamerican myths[/b] that it is almost impossible for us to cover all of them in our game. Moreover, we're hoping that, in time, we [b]will be raising more funds[/b] to help our development process, so that we are able to integrate more characters, beasts, and all kinds of creatures from the Mesoamerican folklore in [i]Mictlan[/i]. 

Remember that [i]Mictlan [/i] is an indie project, we need your support to continue with this laborious and expensive process, your help is invaluable to us!

notes.title: The Patron of All
notes.content:
[h3]Are you wondering who this mysterious, hooded, spectral-looking man is...?[/h3]

He is none other than the [b]apostle Santiago[/b], whose apparitions during the time of the conquest, riding a splendid white horse, astonished all of those who were present. 

Santiago is identified as the [b]patron saint of the conquest[/b] since the Spanish army entrusted their victory to him. 

In ancient writings are recorded [b]Santiago's apparitions[/b], depicting him in shining armor, wielding a sword, with a flowing cloak around his shoulders.

The saint has also a great significance among Mexican people and in a great part of Latin America, it is said that he appeared in Mexico, during the conquest, in the following sites: 

- Centla, currently Tabasco State in 1519; 
- Pedro de Alvarado in Tenochtitlán in 1520; 
- To the troops of Nuño de Guzman, during the the Battle of Tetlán, Jalisco, in 1530; 
- Querétaro, during the conquest of the Chichimecas.

Long after the conquest, he went from being the apostle of the conquerors to being the apostle of the indigenous,[b] patron saint of rain and harvest[/b].

notes.title: The Jaguar Warrior
notes.content:
We are very proud to show you the rendered version of a [b]Jaguar[/b] ([i]ocelotl[/i]) Warrior, who will appear in the game as NPC.

Jaguar Warriors were members of the [b]Aztec military elite[/b]. They had to prove their value and courage on the battlefield by capturing [b]prisoners [/b]and [b]fighting valiantly[/b]. Only then, they could wear the [b]jaguar's tlahuiztli [/b](uniform), a jaguar motif which was associated to [b]Tezcatlipoca [/b]and was also believed to give the warriors the animal's strengths during battles. 

The NPC you see in the video (a [b]work-in-progress[/b]) was knighted "jaguar" by [b]Ahuitzotzin [/b]for his distinguished service in the [b]Tzicoac campaign[/b]. Since then, he participated in many wars, bearing the marks of his battles on his [i]tlahuiztli[/i]. 
The pelt is torn showing his [i]ichcahuipilli [/i]underneath, a leather band is tied around his knee after suffering from a severe injury and, in a fierce battle, his [i]cuatepoztli [/i](helmet) was split open due to a powerful strike. 

For this Jaguar Warrior, every mark, every scar is an [b]emblem of pride[/b], that's why he decided to display them boastfully on his uniform... maybe it's also possible that, with the old age, he's become[b] a bit sentimental[/b]...?

[h3]What do you think? Let us know in the comments![/h3]

notes.title: The Wetlands
notes.content:
Greetings to our [i]Mictlan[/i]'s community!

Today we want to show you one of the [b]biomes [/b]that will be a part of our open world: the [b]wetlands[/b]. 

Mesoamerica is a region abundant in wetlands such as swamps, marshlands and estuarios. These territories with a [b]rich biodiversity[/b] were widely exploited since the arrival of the first nomadic human populations to the continent, with activities like fishing, hunting and gathering of both plants and shellfish. 

The important role this ecosystem played in the[b] development of prehispanic culture[/b] inspired us to recreate this kind of location so that the players may experience the [b]beauty [/b]and the [b]uniqueness [/b]of this environment. 

These screenshots are [b]real-time renders [/b]from our open world, without RTX Ray Tracing. This is what the scenarios will look like in old computer systems and consoles such as the PS4. 

In a couple of months, we will present a [b]technical demo [/b]with our RTX Ray Tracing environments to all of you who want to play [i]Mictlan [/i]on a high-end gaming machine or on the [b]latest generation consoles[/b] such as the Playstation 5.

notes.title: Xochipilli
notes.content:
[b]Xochipilli[/b], the "flower prince" in Nahuatl, is the God of dance, music, arts, drunkenness, carnal love and, in his [i]Macuilxochitl [/i](5 flower) form, the patron of the game [i]patolli[/i]. 

Everyone in ancient Mexico had a God who protected and guided them, in exchange for sacrificial offerings. Xochipilli, in particular, is a God closely tied to [b]sexuality[/b], [b]homosexuality [/b]and [b]bisexuality[/b].

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/4f5d8c288bee6465f2af9bb0f5db23d73340caca.jpg[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/b87400066b0d81a547a88d39ad46c25a9809848f.jpg[/img]

[b]Sahagún [/b]describes him with a [b]floral headdress[/b], which reflects his role as patron of music and songs, his body lightly painted in [b]red[/b], his figure adorned with [b]jade[/b], [b]turquoise [/b]and [b]mother-of-pearl[/b]. 

[b]His statue[/b], which was unearthed on the side of the volcano [i]Popocatépetl [/i]near [i]Tlalmanalco[/i], is decorated with carvings of different type of [b]flowers[/b], such as the [i]ololiuhqui [/i]and the tobacco flower, as well as [i]teonanácatl[/i], also known as the [b]Flesh of the Gods[/b], which is a psychotropic mushroom usually eaten during the festivities and sacrifice, inducing an [b]altered state of consciousness[/b] in their users.

As a matter of fact, his[b] trance-like face[/b] carved in the statue has been interpreted as being in a state of [b]spiritual ecstasy[/b].

notes.title: The great market of Tlatelolco
notes.content:
The [b]great market of Tlatelolco[/b] was one of the largest commercial exchange centers of ancient Mexico before the European conquest. It was founded alongside the city of Tlatelolco in the [b]year 1337[/b], and for a time it rivaled its neighbor and twin city, [b]Tenochtitlan[/b], until it was conquered by Mexica Tlatoani Axayacatl in the year 1473. 

Since then, it became a very important [b]commercial center[/b], where people from the basin of the Valley of Mexico traded intensely, and merchants arrived continuously from [b]all corners of Mesoamerica[/b] to exchange their products. 

The level of [b]organization [/b]and [b]variety of products[/b] was such that it astonished the Spanish conquerors.

[b]Hernán Cortés[/b], in one of his letters, wrote about the market: 
[h3][i]
This city has many public squares where there is continuous trading, buying and selling. There is another square – twice as big the city of Salamanca – even surrounded by portals, where every day there are over sixty thousand souls buying and selling….[/i][/h3]

Take a look at the concept art by [b]Josue Diaz[/b], a talented artist from our team, of the great market of Tlatelolco which we are recreating in [i]Mictlan[/i], bringing to life this key location for exchanging goods in ancient Mexica civilization.

notes.title: Amoxoaque
notes.content:
The [b]Amoxoaque[/b] were [b]great sages[/b] who, since ancient times, used to make their rituals in the sacred city of Teotihuacan. It is said that the Amoxoaque came to our land during the [b]dark times[/b]. They arrived by boat to Panoayan and, from there, started a[b] long pilgrimage[/b] to Tamoanchan, near Teotihuacan, where they finally settled down. 

Today, only [b]four sages [/b]remain among us: Oxomoco, Cipactonal, Tlaltetequi and Xochicauaca, who knew the art of [b]reading the stars[/b] and [b]dreams[/b]. 
 
The recent oral tradition depicts these ancient creatures as [b]tree people [/b]who protect [b]forests [/b]and [b]jungles[/b], that's why our concept art team decided to focus on this element to represent the Amoxoaque. 

Take a look at the stunning work by [b]Jorge H Flores[/b], who managed to combine history and fantasy, bringing these [b]colossal creatures[/b] to life. On their rough bark-like skin you can also see the ancestral engravings from the [b]Cascajal slate[/b], one of the oldest writing expressions in Mesoamerica.

notes.title: Tlahuelpuchi
notes.content:
Today we are presenting to you one of many [b]terrifying creatures[/b] you'll have to face in the dangerous world of [i]Mictlan[/i].

[h3]Tlahuelpuchi: a blood-sucking creature.[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/2e6a2523078edd3208b1003c4ccb07f0f97c522a.jpg[/img]

The Tlahuelpuchi are mythological beings of [b]Tlaxcala folklore[/b], whose origin is still debated among specialists.

Usually female, these creatures were [b]born with a curse[/b] that would accompany them forever. 
The witches had the ability to transform themselves into several animals, such as buzzards, cats, dogs and turkeys. The power to [b]shape-shift[/b] usually came around the age of puberty. At this time, the young Tlahuelpuchi began to crave human blood. 

Their [b]bloodthirst[/b] could only be satisfied by feeding on the blood of [b]infants[/b], who they kidnapped from their rural communities, fleeing to the mountains. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/a16c4ef46d4361a9ac098e0f2e34b322323a680b.jpg[/img]

One of the places where the Tlahuelpuchi met to plot their evils, were the ruins of the[b] temple of Teopanzolco[/b], which was located between Atla and Xolotla, over a hill where, at night, you could see a long line of [b]fireballs[/b]: one of the forms that the Tlahuelpuchi used in order to travel over the skies.

These creatures could actually also [b]live incognito[/b] in their villages, that's why, even in modern folklore, couples with children and women with unbaptized babies [b]protect themselves [/b]and their families by putting orange branches on the roof or their clothes upside down near the crib of the infant, or even by positioning cross-shaped objects under it.

As a matter of fact, the belief in these otherwordly beings has[b] remained alive[/b] until well into the twentieth century in some villages in Mexico. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/8f099501207ea502bce481a03e277cef473f4551.jpg[/img] [img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/192335d4cf51442ed25917e22539e09a0d1f17b2.jpg[/img]

In [i]Mictlan[/i], the Tlahuelpuchi will be [b]adversaries for you to defeat[/b]. 

For their design, we seek to recreate lunar elements, referring to figures such as the [b]goddess Coyolxauhqu[/b]i and the [b]Tzitzimimes[/b], which are the most common inspirations for contemporary Tlahuelpuchi.

notes.title: RE:VIVE
notes.content:
So far, we've been creating the characters who will populate the world of [i]Mictlan [/i]using the sketches and drawings of our talented[b] concept art team[/b], along with [b]artificial intelligence[/b] to shape the faces of Mesoamerican people, obtaining amazing and realistic results.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/f18b345bf08fe428ddd54fe75bdfb6bb78df99ca.jpg[/img]

[h3]But we want to [b]step this process up[/b].[/h3]

As our world becomes more and more connected through technological advances, it's becoming increasingly easy to get in touch with other people and cultures in different countries. The concept of diversity encompasses [b]acceptance[/b], [b]respect [/b]and [b]valorization[/b], understanding that each individual is unique. 

[h3][b]We want to capture[/b] the beauty and uniqueness of [b]indigenous people[/b], that's why we're very proud to launch our ambitious project called [b]RE:VIVE[/b].[/h3]

We're looking for [b]photographers[/b], [b]directors [/b]and any other artist who would like to collaborate with us in order to give us the opportunity to create even more realistic characters, [b]representing the Mexica civilizations[/b] as they properly deserve, through the use of photographs and 3d scanned photogrammetry rendering model.

[h3]It's not just about the game. [/h3]

The heart of the entire development process of [i]Mitclan [/i] lies on the [b]celebration of indigenous cultures[/b], by reviving thousand-years-old tales. 
Our goal with the project RE:VIVE is to [b]preserve the beauty[/b], the [b]uniqueness [/b]and the [b]culture [/b]of a civilization while creating an image data bank for future generations to see. 

Our [b][i]Mictlan [/i]agents[/b] will do so much more than capturing images and video: they will help our community to create a [b]powerful network [/b]of knowledge, beliefs, and people, under the [i][i]Mictlan [/i][/i]umbrella.

We will work with the [b]utmost respect[/b] toward our subjects, their communities, cultures and traditions.
Our mission is to allow people from all over the world to get to know Mexican and Mesoamerican history, [b]valuing our rich heritage[/b], ancient culture, practices but, most of all, [b]our people[/b].

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/be86cf7d282fe3d7e653cdc61f47431a83f27e9d.png[/img]

If anyone is interested in learning more about our RE:VIVE project, please contact us through one our official channels.

Stay tuned for more updates!

notes.title: Xoloitzcuintli
notes.content:
Today we're introducing you to a very[b] special companion[/b]. 

The faithful one who has been accompanying mankind for at least[b] 3,000 years[/b]. 
The one that will be by your side in your adventures in [i][b]Mictlan[/b][/i].

[h3]The very special creature we're talking about is the [b]Xoloitzcuintli[/b]. [/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/ab7c279e37186b6eac394b7fb0db82c99b87eece.jpg[/img]

The Xoloitzcuintli, or[b] Mexican Hairless dog[/b], is one of the oldest and rarest dog breeds in the world. 
It received its name from the Aztec god [b]Xolotl [/b]who, according to the myth, created the dog to guard the living and, most importantly, to [b]guide the souls of the dead[/b] through the dangers of [i]Mictlán[/i], the Underworld. 

Legend has it that, when creating The Fifth Sun, [b]Xolotl[/b] and [b]Quetzalcoatl [/b]descended to the Underworld to [b]collect bones of ancient humans[/b], which they used to restore mankind. The Xoloitzcuintli was created from those same bones and presented as a [b]gift from the gods to humans[/b].

Xoloitzcuintli was not only a faithful companion in life, but it accompanied men in the dangerous journey through the Underworld, the place where the souls of the dead went in their [b]afterlife[/b].
The deceased souls and their dog companion would wander side by side, traveling through the [b]nine levels [/b]of the Underworld for four years, before finally reaching their [b]ultimate destination[/b]: Mictlan.

They had to overcome a series of obstacles and challenges in order to [b]ultimately free their soul[/b].

[h3]Take a look at our WIP of the Xoloitzcuintli![/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/44535ad5bfccca20bad063332f0b1a8e18eb710b.jpg[/img]
